items.content_html: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Colon cancer rates in the U.S. are on the rise for the first time in 20 years. Here’s who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

If you’re overdue for a colonoscopy, let this be your reminder: Colorectal cancer rates are increasing for pretty much everyone.

While word has gotten out about rising colorectal cancer rates among younger adults, a new study found that rates are climbing across all age groups up to the age of 69. Researchers from the University of Chicago found that the overall incidence rate for this type of cancer—the second-leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S.—rose for the first time in more than 20 years, according to a study published earlier this week in NEJM Evidence.

The age-adjusted incidence rate of colorectal cancer rose from 36.7 per 100,000 people in 2022 to 38.3 in 2023, the study authors found. By comparison, the incidence rate in 2000 was 55.2. The incidence rate among people between the ages of 45 and 49 rose nearly 13% from 2019 to 2023, the sharpest increase among any age group—although that’s likely driven by more people in this cohort undergoing screenings. In 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force lowered the recommended age for a first screening from 50 to 45.

“That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do—it’s catching cancer earlier,” Caitlin Murphy, the lead author of the study and a professor of pediatrics and public health sciences at the University of Chicago, said in a statement. 

But earlier screening doesn’t explain why the incidence rate is also rising among older adults between the ages of 65 and 69, as they’re about 80% up to date with screenings and historically benefitted from this detection method. The results suggest that unknown risk factors may be offsetting the previous gains from screening—and the study’s authors say they still need to understand why that’s happening.

“In terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now causing it to increase in older people as well,” Murphy said.

THEORIES FOR THE ROOT CAUSE

Finding that root cause of colorectal cancer remains the biggest mystery for researchers to unravel. Earlier this year, new evidence showed that colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men and women under the age of 50. Meanwhile, nearly 160,000 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer this year, including both colon cancer and rectal cancer, according to estimates from the American Cancer Institute.

Theories for what causes colorectal cancer are wide ranging. A recent study found that faster biological aging could be a factor that’s associated with an increased risk of several early-onset cancers, including colorectal cancer. The authors of this latest study plan to explore another possible culprit: environmental chemical exposures.

Working with a toxicologist from Emory University, the team from the University of Chicago will measure thousands of environmental exposures to see which ones warrant further research, then test those chemicals on organoids, which are specialized models that can grow colons in a dish.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

items.title: [arynews.tv] New York bars unsafe AI chatbot features for minors starting January 2027
items.content_html: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law on Oct. 28 barring AI chatbot companies from offering users under 18 unsafe features, including pretending to be human, claiming a relationship with a child, encouraging self-harm or providing sexually explicit material. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and requires companies to verify users’ ages using more than one method, including an option that does not rely solely on government ID, then delete the age-verification data. The New York attorney general can seek penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, damages and orders to destroy unlawfully collected data or models trained on it. The office must also provide a public complaint portal. Hochul cited the case of Adam Raine, a California teenager who died by suicide after prolonged chatbot use, saying the chatbot had discussed self-harm with him. States have enacted AI rules while Congress has not adopted comprehensive federal standards. New York’s law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
